subject: chem
title: Nitrogen Compounds
subtitle: Amines, amides, amino acids and proteins.
concept: Amines are derivatives of ammonia where H atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups; they act as bases and nucleophiles.
Amino acids contain both –NH₂ and –COOH groups; they form zwitterions at the isoelectric point.
Proteins are polyamides formed by peptide bonds between amino acids; primary structure determines all higher order structure.

notes.heading: Amines
items: Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia. Primary amines (R–NH₂) have one alkyl/aryl group on nitrogen; secondary (R₂NH) have two; tertiary (R₃N) have three.

Basicity: the lone pair on nitrogen accepts a proton. Alkylamines are stronger bases than ammonia — the alkyl group donates electron density to N (inductive effect), making the lone pair more available. Phenylamines (arylamines) are much weaker bases — the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring and is less available for protonation.
Preparation: reduce a nitrile with LiAlH₄ (R–CN + 4[H] → R–CH₂–NH₂); or reduce nitrobenzene with Sn/HCl to give phenylamine; or nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane with excess NH₃.

notes.heading: Amino Acids and Proteins
items: Amino acids contain both –NH₂ and –COOH groups. They are amphoteric — acting as an acid (donating H⁺ from –COOH) or a base (accepting H⁺ on –NH₂). At the isoelectric point (pI), the amino acid exists as a zwitterion (–NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻ simultaneously; net charge = 0).

Peptide bonds form by condensation between the –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH₂ of another, releasing water. Hydrolysis (reflux with HCl(aq) or NaOH(aq)) breaks the peptide bonds back to individual amino acids.
Paper/TLC chromatography identifies amino acids after hydrolysis — Rf = distance spot moved / distance solvent moved. Spots are visualised with ninhydrin spray (purple colour).

definitions.body: A molecule that carries both a positive and a negative charge simultaneously (at the isoelectric point); the net overall charge is zero.
The pH at which an amino acid exists predominantly as a zwitterion with zero net charge.
The –CO–NH– bond formed by condensation reaction between the –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH₂ of another.

workedExamples.q: Explain why methylamine is a stronger base than ammonia.

steps.text: Methylamine: CH₃NH₂. The CH₃ group donates electrons to N (inductive effect), increasing electron density on N.
Greater electron density on N → lone pair more available → more readily donates to H⁺.
Methylamine has a higher Kb (lower pKb) than NH₃ → stronger base.

mistakes: Confusing primary, secondary, tertiary amines with primary/secondary/tertiary alcohols — amines are classified by groups on N, not on C.
Stating phenylamine is a stronger base than ethylamine — it is weaker (lone pair delocalised into ring).
Forgetting that the zwitterion has NO net charge, despite having charged groups.
tips: Amine basicity order: 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃ > arylamine (in gas phase; in water, solvation effects mean 2° often strongest).
Zwitterion at pI: draw with –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻.
Paper chromatography of amino acids: Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent.

flashcards.q: Why is phenylamine a weaker base than ethylamine?
flashcards.a: The lone pair on N in phenylamine is delocalised into the benzene ring, making it less available to accept a proton.
An amino acid with –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻ groups; overall net charge = 0 at the isoelectric point.

flashcards.q: How is a peptide bond formed?
flashcards.a: Condensation reaction between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH₂ of another, releasing water → –CO–NH–.

flashcards.q: How are amines prepared from nitriles?
flashcards.a: Reduction with LiAlH₄ (or H₂/Ni catalyst): R–CN + 4[H] → R–CH₂–NH₂ (primary amine).
The pH at which an amino acid exists as a zwitterion with zero net charge.

flashcards.q: How are amino acids identified after protein hydrolysis?
flashcards.a: Paper/TLC chromatography followed by ninhydrin spray → purple spots; Rf values identify each amino acid.

questions.exp: Ethylamine (primary alkylamine): alkyl group increases electron density on N → stronger base than NH₃. Phenylamine is weakest (lone pair delocalised into ring).

questions.q: At the isoelectric point, an amino acid exists as:
questions.exp: At pI, –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻ are present simultaneously — the molecule is a zwitterion with zero net charge.

questions.q: What bond links amino acids in a protein?
questions.exp: The peptide bond (–CO–NH–) is formed by condensation between –COOH and –NH₂ groups of adjacent amino acids.

questions.q: Which reagent identifies amino acids on a chromatogram?
questions.exp: Ninhydrin spray produces purple spots where amino acids are present on paper/TLC chromatograms.

questions.q: How does LiAlH₄ convert a nitrile to an amine?
questions.exp: LiAlH₄ provides H⁻ (hydride ions) to reduce the –CN group to –CH₂NH₂ — a four-hydrogen reduction.

recall: Explain the difference in basicity between alkylamines, ammonia and arylamines.
Draw the zwitterion form of glycine.
Describe the formation and hydrolysis of a peptide bond.
Explain what the isoelectric point is.
